newsitem.title: ALBANIA: West steps up pressure on Albanian government.
newsitem.headline: West steps up pressure on Albanian government.

text.p: Western countries intensify efforts to resolve the armed rebellion in the south of Albania on Saturday by launching a European security mission headed by former Austrian chancellor Franz Vranitzky.
Vranitzky was due to hold talks with President Sali Berisha, affter overcoming some resistance to his visit as the head of a delegation from the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe.

His visit followed initiatives this week by the European Union and Council of Europe to persuade Albania's embattled leader to halt the resumption of a military campaign to crush rebels who control several southern towns.
Reuters correspondents in southern Albania said chaos among unruly young militants subsided in at least one Adriatic town, Sarande, after former army officers began organising defences.

But the rebels spurned Berisha's offer of an amnesty if they turned in their weapons during a two-day suspension of the government offensive ending early on Sunday. They vowed to stand their ground until Berisha stepped down.

"There will be no more shooting without reason. Parents will take weapons away from kids under 18," a former army colonel in control of Sarande told a crowd of 3,000 on Friday. "The shops will open and there is nothing to fear."
Vranitzky's mission appeared in trouble earlier this week when he acknowledged that Albanian officials had told him he was not welcome in the Balkan country.
"Our basic aim is to offer help," he said this week. "I have no illusion about the mission not being a very difficult one."

Talks on Friday between Berisha and Dutch Foreign Minister Hans Van Mierlo produced few obvious signs of a breakthrough in two months of violence sparked initially by the collapse of several fraudulent pyramid investment plans.

Van Mierlo, representing the EU's six-month Dutch presidency, told reporters he had urged Berisha to "postpone as long as possible or refrain from violence. I repeatedly said: 'Make it possible for the European Union to help Albania'."

A Council of Europe delegation issued similar statements. Both have also called on the opposition to condemn outright violence in the south and formally take up the seats they won in elections last month.

Berisha may be particularly wary of the 54-member OSCE after its persistent efforts under former Spanish prime minister Felipe Gonzalez forced the government of neighbouring Serbia to recognise opposition wins in local elections.

The delegation was also to include OSCE Secretary General Giancarlo Aragona, U.S. Democrat Party Congressman Eliot Engel of New York and officials from Denmark, Switzerland and Poland. Russia, and officials from three EU states -- the Netherlands, Luxembourg and Ireland -- would also attend.
At least 16 people have died in the past week alone in the port of Vlore, focal point of earlier protests by investors who lost money in the failed investment schemes.
